name: Del Monte
lede: Del Monte is a muted grey-violet from the 1930 Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and the books say nothing about where the name came from.

sections.title: A name without a story
sections.body:
Del Monte is known in our sources only as plate 46 E7 of Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color*, published in 1930 [1]. It sits in the ISCC-NBS system as a "grayish purplish blue", about 6.1 units away [1]. No color book we hold explains the name, and the concordance hits that mention "del Monte" are about other things: a cardinal who patronized Caravaggio, and researchers who reported a mineral, weddellite, on limestone in Venice [2][3]. Neither is the origin of the color, so we leave the origin undocumented. A fruit brand and a place name share the words, but that is a guess without a source.

The cardinal does have a place in color history. Gage notes that Caravaggio's early Roman patron, Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte, had a circle that took a positive view of shadow, and that Caravaggio's breadth of shadow neutralized local colors to an unprecedented degree [2]. The color is not named for him, but a muted violet-grey is a fair picture of that neutralized light.

sections.title: Nearby names
sections.body: The closest named colors are muted purples and blue-greys such as [[slate-purple]], [[grey-purple]] and [[blue-grey]], and the darker [[midnight-blue]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 133 paintings, and in 64 by the stricter within-painting measure [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 48 per cent of those works, meaning it is the cool tone tucked into shadows and dark passages [4].

It peaks in the 1900s, in 1.1 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, about 3.1 times the expected rate, and it is most over-represented in France, at 2.5 times expected [4]. The earliest match is a work of 1457 by Alesso Baldovinetti, [[painting:commons-Q3618168|a portrait panel]], which is 473 years before the name's first record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged, varnished photograph [4].
